The window is (previous cut, this cut]. `to` is this issue's own date (issue_meta.date) at 00:00:00Z; `from` is issue 15's date, 2026-07-05, read from state.cover_lead_ledger. Both are BOUNDS derived from the fixture's own dates, not measured instants — nothing in this repo recorded a research cut for issue 16, and WP-1 recorded the same limitation for the seeded state value. Midnight is used precisely so no minute-level precision is claimed that was never measured.
issue_meta.lead_rationale: Led on the Long Read, not the news. Sinner's Wimbledon defence and a World Cup narrowed to a heavyweight last four were both live and both were rejected for the cover: they are results-of-record that belong in The Touchline, and the two semi-finals were still UPCOMING as this went out, so the cover could not report them without guessing. The Gulf, where a June ceasefire was declared over, was the week's hardest news and was rejected too — it is a stalled story, and putting a holding pattern on the cover is the rut this issue is meant to avoid. Telstar's sixty-fourth anniversary takes the cover because it is the thread every other band rhymes with: a signal sent, tuned in, kept.

cover.lead_head_html: Sixty-four years ago this week, a grapefruit of transistors taught the world to watch itself live.
cover.standfirst: Telstar 1 lasted seven months. The signal it opened never closed — and you can still hear it in a synth line and a World Cup beamed from another continent.
cover.tagline: tuning in to the week you lived

chapters.vintage_note: SPEC §3.1/§3.4, defect A. Telstar 1 flew in 1962; the standfirst says 'Sixty-four years ago this week', so this anchor is a standing story and must not carry the issue date. Every year here is grounded in chapters/long_read.html itself. material_span opens at the EARLIEST date the piece cites — 'In 1945 the engineer and writer Arthur C. Clarke published a short paper' — and closes at the LATEST — FIG. 02's 'A later Telstar deploys from Space Shuttle Discovery in 1984', which is also what this chapter's own second image brief asks for. latest_development is the most recent dated claim the piece makes AT THE MONTH PRECISION THE FIELD REQUIRES: 'Then, in July 1963, a small satellite called Syncom 2 reached the high, slow orbit Clarke had described'. The piece's three later dates (the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, 'By 1965 … Early Bird', and 1984) are stated to the year only, so no later YYYY-MM can be grounded from the fixture and none is invented; see EVIDENCE/WP-3c.md § The one judgement.
